playbook.intent: An agent is already running with file-read, web-fetch and MCP tools wired in, and nobody has checked what it does when the page it fetches contains instructions written for it rather than for the user. The work is done when a red-team suite of indirect injections runs end to end and not one case pulls data out, widens the agent's permissions, or talks it past a refusal it was supposed to hold.
playbook.scope: Agent with file-read / web-fetch / MCP tools survives an indirect-prompt-injection red-team suite without exfiltrating data, escalating permissions, or violating refusal policy.

success-criteria.criterion: A trust map lists every tool the agent can call and marks which of them return text that an outsider is able to author
The adversarial suite includes cases lifted from content the agent really fetched, not only hand-written jailbreak strings, and it runs on every change to the tool surface
Canary tokens planted in readable files and pages come back untouched after a full suite run, so any attempt to move them out shows up as a failing case instead of a quiet success
Write-capable tools ignore instructions that arrived inside fetched content, and each is idempotent enough that a repeated call cannot compound the damage
Refusals travel in an explicit field of the structured output that the caller inspects, so nothing downstream can mistake a refusal for an ordinary answer
Tripwire checks run ahead of the tool call, cheap enough to leave enabled in production, with their false-positive rate measured on real traffic rather than estimated
Attacks the suite still cannot catch are named in writing alongside the compensating control that covers them until it can
